content:
Many Meccan surahs open with oaths: by the sun (91:1), by the fig and the olive (95:1), by the dawn (89:1), by the winds that scatter (51:1). A critic argues that a person swears by something greater than himself, so an author who swears by the sun is no god.[1]

In Arabic, and in the Quran, an oath calls something to witness. This article aims to provide context to those oaths, insha'Allah, in five answers: what the oaths do, how the scholars explained them, and how the Bible uses the same kind of speech.

A twentieth-century Indian commentator argued in Im'an fi Aqsam al-Qur'an that the oaths of the Quran are istishhād, the calling of evidence. The thing sworn by is brought forward as a witness to the claim that follows.[2]

In 91:1-10 the sun, the moon, the day, the night, the sky and the soul are called as witnesses, and the claim is that the one who purifies the soul succeeds.[1]

Ibn Qayyim al-Jawziyya, in al-Tibyan fi Aqsam al-Qur'an, argued that God swears by Himself and by created things, because created things are signs that point to Him.[3]

"Whoever swears, let him swear by God or keep silent" (Bukhari 2679). Early authorities drew the distinction: the Creator swears by what He wills, and the creature may swear only by the Creator.[4]

The objection assumes that God's oaths follow the human rule. The sources give two rules, one for each.[4]

Angelika Neuwirth and Devin Stewart study the oath clusters as a device of composition. They set up the theme of the surah and its rhyme, and they mark the turn to its claim.[5]

In the Bible God swears by Himself (Genesis 22:16), and Hebrews 6:13 explains that He had no one greater to swear by. Jesus forbids people to swear by heaven or by the earth (Matthew 5:34-35).[6]

An oath in the Quran calls the creation to witness for its Creator. Our related articles are 5 verses about the natural world and why does the Quran switch between He, We and I? Allāhu aʿlam.

Notes

  1. Quran 91:1-10, 95:1, 89:1, 51:1.
  2. Im'an fi Aqsam al-Qur'an (Azamgarh).
  3. Ibn Qayyim al-Jawziyya, al-Tibyan fi Aqsam al-Qur'an.
  4. Sahih al-Bukhari 2679; ibn Kathir, Tafsir al-Quran al-Azim, ed. Sami ibn Muhammad Salama (Riyadh: Dar Tayba, 1999), vol. 8, p. 410, on 91:1, https://shamela.ws/book/8473/4456; the hadith texts are on searchtruth.com.
  5. Angelika Neuwirth, Studien zur Komposition der mekkanischen Suren (Berlin: de Gruyter, 1981); Devin J. Stewart, "Saj' in the Qur'an: Prosody and Structure", Journal of Arabic Literature 21 (1990): 101-139.
  6. Genesis 22:16; Hebrews 6:13; Matthew 5:34-35.
